fetched_contents.text: Bipolar Disorder: What It Is, Symptoms & Treatment Bipolar disorder symptoms Bipolar disorder causes episodes that shift your mood, energy and activity levels. These episodes can last days, weeks or months. They’re a clear change from your usual self and can affect your daily life. Not everyone has the same pattern. Some people move between episodes often. Others may stay in one mood state for a long time, with periods of steady mood (euthymia) in between. Signs and symptoms of manic episodes Mania can happen many times over a lifetime or only rarely. Symptoms may include: * Feeling extremely happy or excited * Sudden mood changes, such as going from joyful to angry * Restlessness * Rapid speech and racing thoughts * High energy and little need for sleep * Impulsive or risky behavior * Making big or unrealistic plans * Feeling unusually important or powerful * Hallucinations or delusions You may not see the negative effects of your actions. Mania can also increase suicide risk. Severe episodes may require hospital care. Signs and symptoms of hypomania Hypomania is a milder form of mania. You may feel very good, energized or productive. You may still function well at work or in social settings. You might not notice a problem, but others may see changes in your mood or behavior. A depressive episode may follow hypomania. Signs and symptoms of depressive episodes Depressive episodes are the same as major depression. Symptoms may include: * Deep sadness * Low energy or fatigue * Loss of motivation * Feelings of hopelessness or worthlessness * Loss of interest in things you used to enjoy * Trouble concentrating or making decisions * Crying spells * Irritability * Sleeping too much or too little * Appetite changes * Thoughts of death or suicide If you have thoughts of suicide, call or text the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 (U.S.) right away. Signs and symptoms of a mixed episode Mixed episodes include symptoms of both mania and depression at the same time. You may feel low or hopeless, but also restless, agitated and full of energy. Many people describe mixed episodes as very challenging. What is rapid cycling in bipolar disorder? Rapid cycling is when you have four or more mood episodes (mania or depression) in one year. Different things may trigger it, like: * Addictive substance use * Changes to your sleep routine * Some antidepressant use * Stress Bipolar disorder causes There isn’t one single cause of bipolar disorder. It likely develops because several factors add up over time. * Genetics: Bipolar disorder can run in biological families. Many genes may raise your risk. But having these genes doesn’t mean you’ll definitely develop the condition. * Epigenetics: This is how your lifestyle affects your DNA. Your genes can shift in how active they are based on stress, illness or other life events. * Brain chemistry: You may have differences in neurotransmitters (brain chemicals that help control mood), like dopamine and serotonin. These chemicals affect energy, motivation and emotional balance. * Brain structure and connections: Some brain scans show small differences in certain brain areas and in the connections that help those areas communicate. * Other body and brain changes: Researchers are studying other causes, like how your brain changes over time or how your body handles stress. Some studies also look at cell damage and energy problems inside your brain. These may add to the risk, but don’t act alone. As healthcare providers don’t know what causes this condition, there’s no way to prevent it. Risk factors of bipolar disorder Bipolar disorder can affect anyone. Symptoms often start in your teens or early adulthood, but some people don’t get a diagnosis until later in life. Certain factors may raise your chances of developing it, including: * Childhood trauma (emotional abuse or emotional neglect in childhood) * Family history (genetics play a strong role) * Gene changes (many gene variations link, but no single gene causes it) * Major life challenges (like losing a loved one, going through a divorce or experiencing unemployment) Bipolar disorder affects males and females in similar numbers, but it can affect them in different ways. For example, females may switch moods more quickly. Females may also have more periods of depression than males with this condition. Complications of bipolar disorder Mood episodes may cause the following: * Increased risk of suicide or self-harm * Accidents or injuries during manic or mixed episodes * Problems at work or school, relationship difficulties or financial issues If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 (U.S.) or go to the nearest emergency room. Help is available 24/7. The following conditions commonly happen alongside bipolar disorder: * Anxiety disorders * Heart disease * Migraines * Overweight, obesity or binge eating disorder * Substance use disorders

fetched_contents.text: Mixed States in Bipolar Disorder: Etiology, Pathogenesis and Treatment Abstract Many bipolar disorder patients exhibit mixed affective states, which portend a generally more severe illness course and treatment resistance. In the previous renditions of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual mixed states were narrowly defined in the context of bipolar I disorder, but with the advent of DSM-5 the term “mixed episode” was dropped and replaced by “mixed features” specifier which could be broadly applied to manic, hypomanic and depressive episodes in both the bipolar spectrum and major depressive disorders. This paradigm shift reflected their significance in the prognosis and overall management of mood disorders, so that the clinicians should thoroughly familiarize themselves with the contemporary notions surrounding these conditions. The purpose of this manuscript is to bring to light the current conceptualizations regarding the etiology, pathogenesis and treatment of mixed states. To achieve this goal, in June 2016 an extensive literature search was undertaken using the PubMed database. Some exploratory terms utilized included “mixed states”, “mixed episodes”, “switching”, “rapid cycling” cross referenced with “bipolar disorder”. Focusing on the most relevant and up to date studies, it was revealed that mixed states result from genetic susceptibility in the circadian and dopamine neurotransmission apparatuses and disturbance in the intricate catecholamine-acetylcholine neurotransmission balance which leads to mood fluctuations. The management of mixed states is challenging with atypical antipsychotics, newer anticonvulsants and electroconvulsive therapy emerging as the foremost treatment options. In conclusion, while progress has been made in the neurobiological understanding of mixed states, the currently available therapeutic modalities have only shown limited effectiveness. Keywords: Bipolar Disorder; Depressive Disorder, Major; Acetylcholine; Catecholamines; Dopamine INTRODUCTION Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic psychiatric ailment with typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood. While the index episode may manifest as melancholic depression, hypomanic or manic exacerbations may occur later on in the course of the disease and are the sine qua non of the diathesis. It is a prevalent condition and innumerable people are afflicted globally, irrespective of sex, race and geographic location. Vast numbers of patients follow a pernicious course, with adverse sequelae in the biopsychosocial realm. Negatively influencing the prognosis are such factors as repeated mood episodes, mixed affective symptoms, psychiatric and medical comorbidities. The etiopathology of the illness is still unknown and treatments are mainly palliative rather than curative in nature. A particularly difficult matter in the management of bipolar patients is the occurrence of mixed states and the purpose of the present manuscript is to comprehensively address this issue. The strategy adopted in searching the existing literature is first described, followed by a detailed account of the clinical significance of mixed symptoms. Then, the current conceptualizations regarding the etiology and pathogenesis of mixed states are explained, and finally evidence-based treatment options are discussed. SEARCH STRATEGY In June 2016 the PubMed electronic database was explored using a variety terms, for example “mixed states”, “mixed episode”, “switching”, “rapid cycling” cross-referenced with “bipolar disorder”. A very large number of citations exceeding 1,000 were retrieved with this strategy which included clinical trials, retrospective and prospective studies, animal experiments, review articles and case reports. These covered various aspects like causation, clinical characteristics and management. In order to gain a current perspective, papers published in the last 10 years were selected which still numbered over 500; further, it was noticed that the number of publications has increased several fold in the last decade or so. The abstracts of these articles were read and their pertinence to the topic under discussion was determined. About 100 articles were found to be particularly relevant and were comprised of human and animal studies and review articles, which shed light on the subject from different angles. These were read in full and their reference lists were also consulted. The emerging themes from this endeavor were synthesized in a succinct and applicable style to delineate the modern stance on the etiology, pathogenesis and treatment of mixed affective states in bipolar disorder. MIXED SYMPTOMS IN BIPOLAR DISORDER 1. Historical developments regarding the concept of mixed phenomena In BD, patients suffer from severe mood fluctuations which range from major depressive episodes (MDE) to manic or hypomanic exacerbations. Recognized by Kraepelin and described in the 8th edition of his textbook, mixed states have a high prevalence rate in this ailment.1 Since that era, the definition and conceptualization of mixed states has varied, but with the introduction of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual's 5th edition (DSM-5) in 2013, this notion has crystallized and broadened.2 In the preceding DSM-IV-TR, mixed episode was defined in the context of BD type I as an occurrence typified by the concurrent presence of full manic and depressive phenomena in an individual for at least seven days. This narrow definition was radically modified in DSM-5, with its redefinition that the presence of only three symptoms of opposite mood polarity was sufficient to qualify for the specifier “with mixed features”. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Bipolar disorder Request an Appointment Print Diagnosis To find out if you have bipolar disorder, your evaluation may include: * Physical exam. Your healthcare professional may do a physical exam and lab tests to find any medical problems that could be causing your symptoms. * Mental health assessment. Your healthcare professional may refer you to a psychiatrist, who will talk to you about your thoughts, feelings and behavior patterns. You also may answer a series of questions. With your permission, family members or close friends may be asked to provide information about your symptoms. * Mood charting. You may be asked to keep a daily record of your moods, sleep patterns or other factors that could help make the right diagnosis and get you the right treatment. Diagnosis in children Although children and teenagers with bipolar disorder are diagnosed with bipolar disorder based on the same criteria used for adults, symptoms in children and teens often have different patterns. These patterns may not fit neatly into diagnostic categories. Also, children who have bipolar disorder are often diagnosed with other mental health conditions, such as ADHD or behavior problems. This can complicate a diagnosis. These children may need to see a child psychiatrist with experience in bipolar disorder. Care at Mayo Clinic Our caring team of Mayo Clinic experts can help you with your bipolar disorder-related health concerns. Start Here More Information * Bipolar disorder care at Mayo Clinic * Bipolar disorder in children: Is it possible? * Urinalysis Treatment Treatment is best guided by a medical doctor who diagnoses and treats mental health conditions (psychiatrist) who is skilled in treating bipolar and related disorders. Your care team also may include a psychologist, social worker or psychiatric nurse. Bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition, with treatment directed to manage symptoms. Depending on your needs, treatment may include: * Medicines. Often, you'll need to start taking medicines right away to balance your moods. * Ongoing treatment. You need to take your medicine for the rest of your life — even when you feel better. If you don't keep taking your medicine, your symptoms could come back, or minor mood changes could turn into full-blown mania or depression. * Intensive outpatient programs or a program involving a partial stay in a hospital. These programs provide intensive support and counseling that lasts a few hours per day for several weeks to help you get symptoms under control. * Treatment for alcohol or drug misuse. If you have problems with alcohol or drugs, you'll also need treatment for this misuse. Without this treatment, it can be very hard to manage bipolar disorder. * A hospital stay. Your healthcare professional may recommend that you stay in a hospital if you're behaving dangerously or thinking about suicide, or you've become detached from reality. Clinical picture and diagnostic plausibility

The patient’s pattern of “feeling super high energy and unstoppable for a few days, then crash into complete hopelessness for a while” is **plausibly consistent with a bipolar-related diagnosis**, especially bipolar I or bipolar II disorder, but not definitive on its own. The core features that support this are the presence of both elevated mood/energy and low mood/hopelessness, which align with the classic “highs and lows” structure of bipolar disorder [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic and Mayo Clinic both describe bipolar disorder as involving episodes of high energy/mania or hypomania and low mood/depression, with mood swings that can last days, weeks, or months [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The MedlinePlus article also explicitly notes that bipolar disorder can include severe depression and low energy for several days or weeks, with depressive episodes described as “the same as major depression” [N1-F1].

What supports a bipolar diagnosis:
- The presence of a “super high energy” phase with “unstoppable” feelings is consistent with manic or hypomanic symptoms, including high energy, restlessness, rapid speech, impulsive behavior, and a sense of being unusually powerful [N1-F1].
- The “crash into complete hopelessness” matches depressive episode features such as deep sadness, low energy or fatigue, loss of motivation, feelings of hopelessness or worthlessness, and suicidal thoughts [N1-F1].
- The pattern of alternating high and low mood states is a central diagnostic feature of bipolar disorder, even if it is not fully complete [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].

What weakens a straightforward bipolar diagnosis:
- The description is brief and self-reported, so it lacks duration, frequency, and detail needed for a precise diagnosis [N1-F1].
- It does not explicitly include core manic symptoms such as grandiosity, racing thoughts, reduced need for sleep, or risky behavior, which are important in establishing a full manic episode [N1-F1].
- It does not specify whether the patient has had prior episodes, a family history of bipolar disorder, or a history of substance use, all of which are clinically important in diagnosis [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Other diagnoses to consider:
- **Depression with mood instability:** The patient’s pattern could reflect major depression with significant mood instability or mixed features, especially if the high-energy episodes are not full mania but rather a “mixed” or hypomanic-like state [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The Mayo Clinic’s bipolar overview also notes that mixed episodes can include both manic and depressive symptoms at the same time, which may feel like “very challenging” mood swings [N1-F1].
- **Anxiety or stress-related mood symptoms:** The patient’s stress is relevant here. Stress can trigger mood swings, manic episodes, or depressive episodes, and behavioral mediators of stress can contribute to mood instability in both unipolar and bipolar disorders [N5-R2][N5-R3]. This makes anxiety, adjustment disorder, or stress-related mood symptoms plausible explanations, especially if the pattern is recent or linked to a specific stressor [N5-R2][N5-R3].
- **ADHD:** The patient’s “unstoppable” energy and intense focus might be mistaken for ADHD, but ADHD is not typically associated with the crash into hopelessness and the episodic mood shifts that are central to bipolar disorder [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Still, ADHD can co-occur with bipolar disorder and may need to be considered if other features are present [N1-F1].
- **Substance use disorder or sleep disturbance:** The evidence notes that sleep changes and substance use can trigger rapid cycling or mood episodes [N1-F1]. If the patient has any substance use history, sleep issues, or recent life stress, that should be explored carefully [N1-F1][N5-R2].

Overall, the pattern is suggestive of a bipolar-related diagnosis, but the evidence is too limited to be certain. It is important to gather more history about episode frequency, duration, prior episodes, family history, and any substance use, as those details are central to diagnosis [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Treatment options and decision-making

Therapy can be a critical part of treatment for someone with mood instability. The Mayo Clinic explicitly states that the main treatments for bipolar disorder include medicines and talk therapy (psychotherapy) to control symptoms [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Therapy helps by improving coping, managing stress, identifying triggers, and supporting long-term stability [N5-R4][N5-R2]. In particular, the evidence emphasizes that stress management techniques such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, deep breathing exercises, and regular physical activity can help maintain mood stability [N5-R4]. For someone experiencing rapid cycling or mixed symptoms, therapy may also help avoid overuse of antidepressants and support adherence to a broader treatment plan [N1-F1][N3-R3].

Common medications used in bipolar disorder and when they are considered:

Mood stabilizers are the core medication class for bipolar disorder. The Mayo Clinic lists lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine as examples, and notes that mood stabilizers help control manic or hypomanic episodes and may help depressive bouts [N3-F3]. The UptoDate article similarly lists lithium, valproate, quetiapine, and lamotrigine as second-line options for maintenance treatment [N3-R4]. Antipsychotics such as olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, and others are also used as mood stabilizers and may be used alone or with mood stabilizers [N3-F3]. Antidepressants are mentioned cautiously because they may cause manic or hypomanic episodes and should be used only with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3]. The CANMAT/ISBD guidelines note that augmentation therapy with antipsychotics and mood stabilizers is more effective than monotherapy [N3-R5].

When medications are considered:
- Acute episodes are typically managed with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics that can stabilize mood quickly [N3-F3].
- Depressive episodes may sometimes include a cautious antidepressant, but only in combination with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3].
- Rapid cycling or mixed symptoms may require more aggressive or combination treatment, as no single medication is effective against all phases of bipolar disorder [N3-R3].
- Long-term maintenance treatment is usually needed because bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition [N3-F3].

Risks, benefits, and realistic expectations:

Benefits:
- Medications can reduce the severity and frequency of mood episodes, improve functioning, and reduce suicide risk [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- Therapy can improve coping, reduce relapse, and support adherence to medication [N3-R2][N5-R4].
- Combined treatment is often more effective than medication alone [N3-R5].

Risks:
- Medications may have side effects, and finding the right one often requires trial and error [N3-F3].
- Antidepressants can sometimes trigger mania or hypomania, so they are used cautiously [N3-F3].
- Long-term use may require blood monitoring and dose adjustments [N3-F3].
- Medication alone may not fully eliminate mood instability, especially if other stressors or comorbid conditions are present [N1-F1][N5-R2].

Realistic expectations:
- Bipolar disorder is not cured by medication alone; it is managed with long-term treatment [N3-F3].
- Therapy can take time to produce noticeable effects and may need to be combined with medication [N3-F3].
- Stress reduction and lifestyle changes can improve outcomes, but they should not replace professional care [N5-R4][N5-R2].
- Rapid cycling or mixed episodes may require more intensive treatment, including hospitalization if needed [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In short, therapy and medication are both important, with medication usually used first for acute stabilization and therapy for ongoing support and stress management [N3-R2][N3-F3][N5-R4].

Differential diagnosis and diagnostic uncertainty

Other conditions that could explain mood swings and stress-related crashes include:

1. **Major depression with mixed features or mood instability:** If the patient’s “high energy” episodes are not full mania but rather a mixed state, this could still be a plausible explanation. Mixed episodes include both manic and depressive symptoms at the same time, and the Mayo Clinic notes that mixed episodes can be very challenging [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The mixed-state literature also emphasizes that mixed symptoms are common in bipolar disorder and may be especially difficult to treat [N2-F2].

2. **Anxiety disorders or adjustment disorder:** Anxiety can produce mood instability, and the evidence states that stress can trigger mood swings, manic episodes, or depressive episodes [N5-R2]. Behavioral mediators of stress can also contribute to mood symptoms in both unipolar and bipolar disorders [N5-R3]. Anxiety may explain the “stress-related crashes,” while the high-energy periods may resemble hypomania or excitement from anxiety [N5-R2][N5-R3].

3. **ADHD:** The patient’s “unstoppable” energy and intense focus may be mistaken for ADHD, especially if the mood crashes are not as severe or episodic as in bipolar disorder. However, ADHD is not typically associated with the depressive crashes and episodic mood shifts that are central to bipolar disorder [N1-R1][N1-F1]. That said, ADHD can co-occur with bipolar disorder and should be considered if other features are present [N1-F1].

4. **Substance use disorder or sleep disturbance:** The evidence notes that sleep changes and substance use can trigger rapid cycling or mood episodes [N1-F1]. This makes substance use, caffeine use, or sleep disruption important to rule out, especially if the pattern is recent or worsened after a life change [N1-F1][N5-R2].

5. **Other mood disorders or personality-related issues:** The Mayo Clinic notes that bipolar disorder is not the only mood disorder and that other conditions such as ADHD or behavior problems can complicate diagnosis in children [N4-F4]. While the patient’s age is not specified, the principle remains that overlapping diagnoses can make bipolar disorder harder to distinguish from depression, anxiety, or ADHD [N4-F4].

How primary care and specialists differ in diagnosing uncertain cases:

Primary care physicians often first encounter bipolar disorder because patients may present with mood symptoms before they see a psychiatrist [N4-F4]. However, the evidence also notes that primary care physicians may have a low index of suspicion and that bipolar disorder can be difficult to diagnose because of its diverse symptoms and comorbid conditions [N4-F4]. A thorough diagnostic evaluation is essential, including clinical interview, case-finding tools, and support from family members or close friends [N4-F4]. The evidence also says that in cases of continued diagnostic uncertainty, a follow-up interview by an experienced primary care provider may be needed [N6-R1]. Specialists, especially psychiatrists, are better equipped to distinguish bipolar disorder from depression or other diagnoses because they can assess for full manic or hypomanic episodes, family history, and treatment response [N4-F4][N4-R4].

What evidence matters most for ruling out or supporting bipolar disorder:

- **Episode pattern:** Duration, frequency, and polarity of mood episodes are central. The evidence emphasizes that bipolar disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes separated by euthymic periods [N4-F4][N1-F1].
- **Manic/hypomanic features:** The presence of elevated energy, restlessness, rapid speech, impulsive behavior, or grandiosity supports a bipolar diagnosis [N1-F1].
- **Depressive features:** Deep sadness, hopelessness, low energy, and suicidal thoughts are consistent with depressive episodes [N1-F1].
- **Family history:** The evidence states that genetics play a strong role and that bipolar disorder can run in biological families [N1-F1][N1-R5].
- **Stress and triggers:** Stress can trigger mood episodes and may explain stress-related crashes, but it is not sufficient alone to diagnose bipolar disorder [N5-R2][N5-R3].
- **Response to treatment:** A specialist can help determine whether treatment response supports or weakens the diagnosis [N4-F4].
- **Rule-out comorbidities:** Anxiety, ADHD, substance use, and sleep problems should be ruled out or considered alongside bipolar disorder [N5-R2][N5-R3][N4-F4].

In uncertain cases, the most important evidence is whether the patient has a full manic or hypomanic episode, how the symptoms relate to stress, and whether other diagnoses can explain the pattern [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R2]. The evidence also highlights that diagnostic uncertainty is common and that follow-up interviews and specialist consultation are often needed [N4-F4][N6-R1].

Next steps and practical advice

Whether to see a therapist, psychiatrist, or primary care doctor first:

- **Primary care doctor first:** The Mayo Clinic recommends starting with a primary care provider, and notes that primary care physicians are often the first point of contact for bipolar disorder [N4-R1][N4-F4]. Stress appears to be a major factor here. The evidence says stress can lead to mood swings, manic episodes, or depressive episodes [N5-R2]. - Keeping a mood chart to track highs, lows, sleep, and stressors [N3-F3].

- **ADHD:** The “unstoppable” energy could be mistaken for ADHD, but ADHD is not typically associated with the depressive crashes and episodic mood shifts that are central to bipolar disorder [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Substance use or sleep disturbance:** The evidence notes that sleep changes and substance use can trigger rapid cycling or mood episodes [N1-F1]. So if your pattern started after a life change, stress, or sleep disruption, that matters.
- **Other mood disorders or comorbid conditions:** Bipolar disorder is not the only mood disorder, and the evidence notes that ADHD and other conditions can complicate diagnosis [N4-F4].

## 4) How to think about diagnostic uncertainty
The branch report makes clear that **diagnostic uncertainty is common** and that **primary care doctors often first see bipolar disorder patients** because the symptoms can be vague or overlap with depression [N4-F4]. The key differences between primary care and specialists are:
- **Primary care:** Often first contact, but may have a low index of suspicion and may need follow-up interviews or specialist input [N4-F4][N6-R1].
- **Specialists:** Psychiatrists are better equipped to assess for full manic or hypomanic episodes, family history, and treatment response [N4-F4][N4-R4].

The evidence says what matters most for ruling out or supporting bipolar disorder is:
- Episode pattern: duration, frequency, and polarity of mood episodes [N4-F4][N1-F1],
- Manic/hypomanic features,
- Depressive features,
- Family history,
- Stress and triggers,
- and whether other conditions can explain the pattern [N1-F1][N4-F4][N5-R2].

## 5) Should you see a therapist or try medication?
The answer is: **both.** The evidence says the main treatments for bipolar disorder include medicines and talk therapy (psychotherapy) to control symptoms [N3-R2][N3-F3]. That means:
- **Medication is usually used first for acute stabilization.** Mood stabilizers, antipsychotics, and sometimes antidepressants are common options, but antidepressants are used cautiously because they can trigger mania or hypomania [N3-F3][N3-R3].
- **Therapy is important for ongoing support and stress management.** Therapy can help improve coping, identify triggers, and support long-term stability [N3-R2][N5-R4].

### Realistic expectations
- Medication can reduce episode severity and improve functioning, but no single medication is effective against all phases of bipolar disorder [N3-R3][N3-R5].
- Therapy can improve coping and reduce relapse, but it may take time and should be combined with medication [N3-R2][N3-F3].
- Stress management techniques such as mindfulness, yoga, deep breathing, and regular activity can help maintain mood stability [N5-R4].
- Rapid cycling or mixed episodes may require more intensive treatment, including hospitalization if needed [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## 6) What should you do next?
### First, see a **primary care doctor** first
The Mayo Clinic recommends starting with a primary care provider, and notes that primary care physicians are often the first point of contact for bipolar disorder [N4-R1][N4-F4]. This is a reasonable first step because primary care can screen for medical problems and refer to specialists if needed [N4-F4].

### Then, see a **psychiatrist** next
If the pattern is strongly suggestive, a psychiatrist should be seen next because they are best equipped to diagnose and manage bipolar disorder, including prescribing medications and monitoring for mania or mixed episodes [N4-R4][N4-F4].

### And consider a **therapist/psychotherapist**
Therapy can be helpful at any stage, especially for coping with stress, managing mood instability, and supporting long-term adjustment [N3-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that psychotherapy and psychosocial treatments are generally used alongside medication [N3-R3].

### What to ask the provider during the first visit
A useful first-visit conversation would include:
- “Could this be bipolar disorder, depression, anxiety, or something else?”
- “What tests or questions do you need to rule out other conditions?”
- “What symptoms would make you think I might have bipolar disorder?”
- “What medications are usually used for this?”
- “Can you explain how long treatment will last and what to expect?”
- “Do you recommend a follow-up interview if the diagnosis is uncertain?” [N4-F4][N4-R4][N5-R4]

## 7) How to manage stress and daily functioning while waiting for help
Stress appears to be a major factor here. The evidence says stress can lead to mood swings, manic episodes, or depressive episodes [N5-R2]. It also notes that stress management techniques such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, deep breathing exercises, and regular physical activity can help maintain mood stability [N5-R4]. Practical steps include:
- Keeping a mood chart to track highs, lows, sleep, and stressors [N3-F3].
- Avoiding substance use, caffeine, or other triggers that may worsen mood swings [N1-F1][N5-R2].
- Using relaxation techniques and physical activity to manage stress [N5-R4].
- Asking a trusted friend or family member to support you and note any changes in behavior [N4-F4].
- Staying connected to social supports and avoiding isolation [N5-R4].

## Bottom line
Your pattern is **plausibly consistent with a bipolar-related diagnosis**, but it is not enough on its own to make a definite diagnosis [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The evidence also shows that **other conditions** such as major depression with mixed features, anxiety, ADHD, substance use, or sleep disturbance should be considered [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3]. 

The best approach is to:
1. **Start with a primary care doctor** [N4-R1][N4-F4].
2. **Follow up with a psychiatrist** if the pattern is strongly suggestive [N4-R4][N4-F4].
3. **Use therapy alongside medication** where appropriate [N3-R2][N3-F3][N5-R4].
4. **Manage stress carefully** and stay connected to support [N5-R4][N5-R2].

If you’re really stressed and worried, that’s normal. The evidence also notes that early, accurate diagnosis can substantially reduce the burden of bipolar disorder and improve long-term outcomes [N4-F4]. So the most important thing is to get help soon, and to keep a clear record of your symptoms while you wait [N3-F3][N5-R4].

The MedlinePlus article also explicitly notes that bipolar disorder can include severe depression and low energy for several days or weeks, with depressive episodes described as “the same as major depression” [N1-F1].

Treatment options and decision-making

Therapy can be a critical part of treatment for someone with mood instability. The Mayo Clinic explicitly states that the main treatments for bipolar disorder include medicines and talk therapy (psychotherapy) to control symptoms [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Therapy helps by improving coping, managing stress, identifying triggers, and supporting long-term stability [N5-R4][N5-R2]. In particular, the evidence emphasizes that stress management techniques such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, deep breathing exercises, and regular physical activity can help maintain mood stability [N5-R4]. For someone experiencing rapid cycling or mixed symptoms, therapy may also help avoid overuse of antidepressants and support adherence to a broader treatment plan [N1-F1][N3-R3].

Common medications used in bipolar disorder and when they are considered:

Mood stabilizers are the core medication class for bipolar disorder. The Mayo Clinic lists lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine as examples, and notes that mood stabilizers help control manic or hypomanic episodes and may help depressive bouts [N3-F3]. The UptoDate article similarly lists lithium, valproate, quetiapine, and lamotrigine as second-line options for maintenance treatment [N3-R4]. Antipsychotics such as olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, and others are also used as mood stabilizers and may be used alone or with mood stabilizers [N3-F3]. Antidepressants are mentioned cautiously because they may cause manic or hypomanic episodes and should be used only with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3]. The CANMAT/ISBD guidelines note that augmentation therapy with antipsychotics and mood stabilizers is more effective than monotherapy [N3-R5].

When medications are considered:
- Acute episodes are typically managed with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics that can stabilize mood quickly [N3-F3].
- Depressive episodes may sometimes include a cautious antidepressant, but only in combination with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3].
- Rapid cycling or mixed symptoms may require more aggressive or combination treatment, as no single medication is effective against all phases of bipolar disorder [N3-R3].
- Long-term maintenance treatment is usually needed because bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition [N3-F3].

Risks, benefits, and realistic expectations:

Benefits:
- Medications can reduce the severity and frequency of mood episodes, improve functioning, and reduce suicide risk [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- Therapy can improve coping, reduce relapse, and support adherence to medication [N3-R2][N5-R4].
- Combined treatment is often more effective than medication alone [N3-R5].

Risks:
- Medications may have side effects, and finding the right one often requires trial and error [N3-F3].
- Antidepressants can sometimes trigger mania or hypomania, so they are used cautiously [N3-F3].
- Long-term use may require blood monitoring and dose adjustments [N3-F3].
- Medication alone may not fully eliminate mood instability, especially if other stressors or comorbid conditions are present [N1-F1][N5-R2].

Realistic expectations:
- Bipolar disorder is not cured by medication alone; it is managed with long-term treatment [N3-F3].
- Therapy can take time to produce noticeable effects and may need to be combined with medication [N3-F3].
- Stress reduction and lifestyle changes can improve outcomes, but they should not replace professional care [N5-R4][N5-R2].
- Rapid cycling or mixed episodes may require more intensive treatment, including hospitalization if needed [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In short, therapy and medication are both important, with medication usually used first for acute stabilization and therapy for ongoing support and stress management [N3-R2][N3-F3][N5-R4].

Anxiety may explain the “stress-related crashes,” while the high-energy periods may resemble hypomania or excitement from anxiety [N5-R2][N5-R3].

3. **ADHD:** The patient’s “unstoppable” energy and intense focus may be mistaken for ADHD, especially if the mood crashes are not as severe or episodic as in bipolar disorder. That said, ADHD can co-occur with bipolar disorder and should be considered if other features are present [N1-F1].

4. **Substance use disorder or sleep disturbance:** The evidence notes that sleep changes and substance use can trigger rapid cycling or mood episodes [N1-F1]. Primary care physicians often first encounter bipolar disorder because patients may present with mood symptoms before they see a psychiatrist [N4-F4]. However, the evidence also notes that primary care physicians may have a low index of suspicion and that bipolar disorder can be difficult to diagnose because of its diverse symptoms and comorbid conditions [N4-F4]. A thorough diagnostic evaluation is essential, including clinical interview, case-finding tools, and support from family members or close friends [N4-F4]. The evidence also says that in cases of continued diagnostic uncertainty, a follow-up interview by an experienced primary care provider may be needed [N6-R1]. Specialists, especially psychiatrists, are better equipped to distinguish bipolar disorder from depression or other diagnoses because they can assess for full manic or hypomanic episodes, family history, and treatment response [N4-F4][N4-R4].

What evidence matters most for ruling out or supporting bipolar disorder:

Therapy can be a critical part of treatment for someone with mood instability. The Mayo Clinic explicitly states that the main treatments for bipolar disorder include medicines and talk therapy (psychotherapy) to control symptoms [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Therapy helps by improving coping, managing stress, identifying triggers, and supporting long-term stability [N5-R4][N5-R2]. Mood stabilizers are the core medication class for bipolar disorder. The Mayo Clinic lists lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine as examples, and notes that mood stabilizers help control manic or hypomanic episodes and may help depressive bouts [N3-F3]. The UptoDate article similarly lists lithium, valproate, quetiapine, and lamotrigine as second-line options for maintenance treatment [N3-R4]. Antipsychotics such as olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, and others are also used as mood stabilizers and may be used alone or with mood stabilizers [N3-F3]. Antidepressants are mentioned cautiously because they may cause manic or hypomanic episodes and should be used only with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3]. The CANMAT/ISBD guidelines note that augmentation therapy with antipsychotics and mood stabilizers is more effective than monotherapy [N3-R5].

When medications are considered:
- Acute episodes are typically managed with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics that can stabilize mood quickly [N3-F3].
- Depressive episodes may sometimes include a cautious antidepressant, but only in combination with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic [N3-F3].
- Rapid cycling or mixed symptoms may require more aggressive or combination treatment, as no single medication is effective against all phases of bipolar disorder [N3-R3].
- Long-term maintenance treatment is usually needed because bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition [N3-F3].

Risks, benefits, and realistic expectations:

Benefits:
- Medications can reduce the severity and frequency of mood episodes, improve functioning, and reduce suicide risk [N1-F1][N3-F3].
- Therapy can improve coping, reduce relapse, and support adherence to medication [N3-R2][N5-R4].
- Combined treatment is often more effective than medication alone [N3-R5].

Risks:
- Medications may have side effects, and finding the right one often requires trial and error [N3-F3].
- Antidepressants can sometimes trigger mania or hypomania, so they are used cautiously [N3-F3].
- Long-term use may require blood monitoring and dose adjustments [N3-F3].
- Medication alone may not fully eliminate mood instability, especially if other stressors or comorbid conditions are present [N1-F1][N5-R2].

Realistic expectations:
- Bipolar disorder is not cured by medication alone; it is managed with long-term treatment [N3-F3].
- Therapy can take time to produce noticeable effects and may need to be combined with medication [N3-F3].
- Stress reduction and lifestyle changes can improve outcomes, but they should not replace professional care [N5-R4][N5-R2].
- Rapid cycling or mixed episodes may require more intensive treatment, including hospitalization if needed [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In short, therapy and medication are both important, with medication usually used first for acute stabilization and therapy for ongoing support and stress management [N3-R2][N3-F3][N5-R4].

Your pattern is still too brief and incomplete to be certain. The evidence emphasizes that bipolar disorder diagnosis depends on:
- Duration and frequency of episodes,
- Whether you have had prior episodes,
- Family history,
- Substance use,
- and other details that help distinguish bipolar disorder from other conditions [N1-F1][N1-R5].
